_comment: Content for /knowledge/accents: varieties of European Portuguese in Portugal (mainland, the Azores, Madeira), Portugal's other languages, and the Portuguese of Brazil, Africa and Timor-Leste as notes. Names, places and examples ([local form, plain English]) are not translated; the descriptions are in public/i18n/en.json under dialekte.r.* (areas), dialekte.m.* (dots), dialekte.w.* (world notes) and dialekte.group.*. Markers with lang: true are languages, not accents. words: `de` holds what the map asks about. lines: `benrath` is the line of the b/v merger (vinho said binho north of it), `speyer` the line where ei becomes ê (peixe said pêxe south of it); the key names are kept from the German page. shift: one row per word, columns in the order of groups. Coordinates for the Azores and Madeira are real; the generator moves them into inset boxes (the Azores at reduced scale). Examples are in European Portuguese spelling (AO90); local pronunciations are written the way a learner would hear them. Geometry: scripts/generate-dialekte-karte.mjs → dialekte-karte.json.

regions.name: Minho and Porto
regions.alias: falares do Minho e do Douro Litoral
say: o vinho: v and b sound the same
a small draught beer (Lisbon: uma imperial)
the ou stays a real diphthong: 'po-u-co', not Lisbon 'pôco'

regions.name: Trás-os-Montes and the Upper Douro
say: a chuva, the rain: some older speakers start ch with a t
Vamos embora! Let's go: b for v
an s made with the tip of the tongue, a little like Madrid

regions.name: Coimbra and the Beiras
say: o leite: ei with a closed e, where Lisbon says 'lâite'
tudo: in some villages of Beira Baixa the u is said with rounded lips, like French u

regions.name: Lisbon and the centre-west
regions.alias: falar de Lisboa, Estremadura e Ribatejo
say: o leite, o peixe: the Lisbon ei sounds like 'ay'
a small draught beer (Porto: um fino)

regions.name: Alentejo
say: o peixe: ei becomes a plain ê
Estou a fazer. The Alentejo uses the gerund, like Brazil. Hear it, don't copy it.

regions.name: Algarve
say: Estou a fazer: the gerund, as in the Alentejo

regions.name: The Azores
say: tudo, muito: on São Miguel the u is said with rounded lips, like French u
the shearwater, the islands' seabird; also a friendly nickname for Azoreans

regions.name: Madeira
say: the island drink: aguardente, honey and lemon

markers.name: Porto speech
say: a strong but friendly exclamation; casual, friends only

markers.name: Lisbon speech
say: really cool (young speakers; bué = very, a lot)

markers.name: Mirandese
markers.where: mirandés · Miranda do Douro and Vimioso, Trás-os-Montes
say: the Mirandese language (Portuguese: a língua mirandesa)

markers.name: Barranquenho
markers.where: barranquenho · Barrancos, Alentejo, on the Spanish border

shift: binho: v and b sound the same
pâixe in Lisbon, pêixe in Coimbra
xave; tchave from some older speakers
tudo; tüdo in parts of Beira Baixa
estou a fazer; the gerund is heard too

world.name: Brazil
say: Estás a falar. You're speaking: você and the gerund
Dás-me um café? The pronoun comes first in Brazil.

world.name: Angola
say: very, a lot: bué de gente (Lisbon slang took it over)
an older person, someone you respect
the shared minibus taxi of Luanda

world.name: Cape Verde
say: How are you? (Cape Verdean Creole, Santiago)

world.name: Guinea-Bissau
say: greetings sent to someone: manda mantenhas (Kriol, also Cape Verde)

world.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
say: take it easy: the islands' calm pace, a motto

world.name: Timor-Leste
say: Good morning! (Tetum, the other official language)
